concepts.title: The Grandmother as a Study in Constancy
concepts.definition: Khushwant Singh sketches his grandmother as an unchanging figure -- old even in his earliest memory, wrinkled, bent, silver-haired, forever telling beads of her rosary. Her constancy of appearance mirrors constancy of character: gentle, devout, dignified, and quietly powerful within the household.
concepts.key_idea: A portrait painted in one unchanging pose -- the grandmother's outer stillness expresses inner steadiness.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb101.txt early section (grandmother's appearance, wrinkles, silver hair, rosary, beauty without youth)

solution_steps.explain: Gather the concrete marks: wrinkles across her face, white hair covering it, bent frame, spotless white clothes.
Each detail signals serenity and purity; the winter-landscape image fuses her whiteness with calm.
By fixing her as ageless, the writer makes her the story's moral anchor -- change happens around her, not in her.

concepts.title: The Friendship in the Village and Its Rupture in the City
concepts.definition: In the village the boy and his grandmother were inseparable: she woke him, readied his wooden slate, fed him chapattis thick with butter, and walked him to school attached to the temple. The move to the city snapped the bond -- the English school, its science lessons and its music room left her outside her grandson's world.
concepts.key_idea: Distance begins not with miles but with mismatched worlds -- an English education she could not enter.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb101.txt middle section (village companionship, school attached to temple, city education, english words, music lessons grief)
question_patterns: how was the grandmother's friendship with the author broken in the city

solution_steps.explain: Morning baths, buttered chapattis, the walk to the temple school where her alphabets and his lessons ran side by side.
A shared room ended, the school became unreachable to her, and English words and science seemed foreign ground.
For her, music belonged to beggars and harmonium-playing girls, not gentlefolk -- so the new school sealed her estrangement.

concepts.title: The Sparrows: Silent Mourning at the End
concepts.definition: The story's most striking image closes it: the grandmother, sensing her end, refuses to speak, prays through her last day, and dies with her beads; at sunset thousands of sparrows who fed beside her daily arrive, ignore the scattered crumbs, and fly away silently at dusk -- nature itself in mourning.
concepts.key_idea: Birds that never spoke to her mourn her without sound -- the story's quiet miracle of sympathy.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb101.txt closing section (declining peace, refusal to talk, death with rosary, sparrows' silent vigil, mother breaking crumbs)
question_patterns: how did the grandmother spend her last evening before death
in class 11 the portrait of a lady: describe the scene of the sparrows after the grandmother died

explain the significance of the silent sparrows at the end

solution_steps.explain: Fevered only slightly, she declines further talk, recites prayers and her beads, and lies down to die with composure.
The sparrows that daily squabbled over her crumbs gather silently, ignore her daughter's scattered bread, and depart at dusk.
The birds' fast in silence externalises the family's grief and crowns the grandmother's communion with all living things.

concepts.title: Themes: Ageing, Tradition and Quiet Love
concepts.definition: Beneath its simple narrative, the chapter carries larger themes: the dignity of ageing, the endurance of traditional faith against modern education, and love expressed not in words but in service -- feeding, waking, walking, praying. The story mourns a world where such wordless devotion was daily bread.
concepts.key_idea: Love measured in service, tradition measured in prayer -- the story honours what the modern city leaves behind.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb101.txt whole chapter (themes of affection, tradition versus modernity, dignity of old age, wordless companionship)
question_patterns: what are the main themes of the portrait of a lady

what values does the grandmother embody for the narrator

solution_steps.explain: Count her deeds -- feeding, fetching, praying -- to see affection performed rather than announced.
Set her temple-and-rosary world against the narrator's English schooling to expose the tradition-modernity strain.
Like a painter's portrait, the chapter fixes one figure in one pose; movement belongs to the world around her.

worked_examples.source_ref: kehb101.txt middle section (city school and music)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain why the grandmother, who once walked the boy to school, gradually stopped talking to him in the city.

solution_template.explain: Separate rooms and a school she could not enter ended the shared daily round.
English words, science's unanswerable questions, and music lessons all fell outside her world and her values.
Her silence grew from the gulf between her world of prayer and his world of print -- not from anger but estrangement.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Comment on the appropriateness of ending the chapter with the sparrows' silent departure.

solution_template.explain: Sparrows fed daily beside her -- their bond with her was established through the whole story.
At her death they refuse the crumbs -- an inversion that signals grief more eloquently than tears.
The silent close amplifies the theme of wordless love and leaves the reader in the same hush as the courtyard.
